name: Amira Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary day at the agency look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the visual work in a six-person studio, mostly food packaging and clinic leaflets. I have a master’s in design, so I catch the expensive little mistakes before files go to print; last week a missing allergy line stopped a label run. The pay is oddly low for a lead, and after rent I have about three weeks of expenses saved.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day do you look forward to?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The proof from the printer, when the colour and the words finally match what the client meant. I use an AI image tool now and then to try a rough concept, but the final layout is my responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the studio that AI Plateau sounds much like the rough-image tool we already have: useful for a quick sketch, useless for the allergy warning. I would still want a person to sign off the print proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead work stays, but the agency's low wage is already the problem. Eli's café shifts vary, and our three-week buffer would vanish if the printer billed us for a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep signing off food labels against the original client copy and ask the owner for a written review of my lead pay. In the first year of small AI change, I would put any raise into a separate rent buffer instead of replacing my old laptop immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, fairly settled about the design work. A quiet AI year will not make a rent payment for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the mistake you are most careful about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small café changed its nut supplier, but the approved label still said nut-free. I caught the old wording on the signed source sheet before the printer ran the boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Eli be able to cover rent if your pay stayed flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eli (my partner) has regular café shifts but fewer in a slow week. I would not count a busy weekend as a second salary.

say: I would tell colleagues **print proof** still needs a human sign-off.
I would say the rough-image tool saves **sketch time**, not client responsibility.
think: I believe my **lead work** stays in this picture.
I worry our **three-week buffer** is too thin for rent and variable café shifts.
do: Keep **checking labels** against original client copy in 2026 and the first year.
Ask the owner for a **written pay review**; save any raise for rent.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about existing money pressure, though design work looks stable.
S0.quote: A quiet AI year will not make a rent payment for us.
fieldNote: Her **design authority** comes from catching print errors rather than producing more sketches.
The agency wage and Eli’s variable café shifts leave **little cash** even without major AI change.

steps.text: Check food labels against signed client copy before print
Request written lead-pay review and save any raise for rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the agency might sell fewer hours for first drafts when AI can write and lay out a leaflet. At work I would ask whether that saving pays for proper proofing or just a smaller design team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could keep the final proof work, but I could lose two paid design days as clients buy cheaper concepts. I cannot make that gap up with Eli's uneven café wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would collect six recent jobs where the client's first copy changed at the print stage and show the owner the correction hours. In the first year routine layouts move, I would ask for my weekly paid hours in writing and compare posted production-art roles; I would apply only if the listed wage and hours cover rent after the bus fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because I can see a useful role and a shorter payslip at the same time. The printer does not pay me for being right unless the agency keeps my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn a new design tool for this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the agency buys the new AI-powered layout system, I would learn its preflight checks on paid time by testing three old jobs with known errors. I would not call an unpaid weekend of tutorials a job plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in a production-art advert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The written weekly hours, wage and bus journey first. A title that pays for two days when rent needs five is not an opening I can use.

say: I would ask whether faster **first drafts** preserve paid proofing hours.
I would question whether cheap **first drafts** simply mean a smaller design team.
think: I could keep proof responsibility but lose **paid design days**.
I cannot replace missing wages with Eli’s **variable café pay**.
do: Show the owner **six correction records** now and request written paid hours when routine layouts move.
Test the new **preflight checks** on three old jobs on paid time if the agency buys the system.
Compare posted **production-art roles** and apply only on rent-covering weekly wage and hours after bus fare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fewer paid days despite useful proofing skill.
S1.quote: The printer does not pay me for being right unless the agency keeps my hours.
fieldNote: She distinguishes the value of **error correction** from whether a small agency will keep paying for it.
She would learn an actual **new preflight system** only if bought and practised on paid time.

steps.text: Show six correction records and request written weekly design hours
Test new AI preflight checks on three old jobs if bought, on paid time
Apply for posted production-art roles only with after-bus rent-covering weekly wage and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the six of us that full AGI by 2028 could make a client's entire campaign file before we can quote for it. Robots around 2031 are not much comfort to a designer whose work lives on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the agency to lose most layout fees, and my lead title may not protect a wage at all. Three weeks saved and only a few local studios leave Eli and me almost no room for a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would ask the owner for written client-booking and staffing plans, and list the print shops I can reach by bus. If most paid design work ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply for a posted paid print-production post and keep any agency hours still offered; I would accept only written full-week wages and hours covering rent and fares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed; I can feel myself counting how many rent dates fit into three weeks. A master's degree cannot be cashed at the landlord's desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you offer a print shop that AGI does not settle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how to check a physical proof against a signed colour sample and stop a bad run. I would ask to see the paid production duties before claiming I can run the press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for press training now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not out of this buffer. If a posted paid post required a press-safety course and the shop covered the fee and paid the training hours, I would take it; otherwise I would keep applying for work I can already do.

say: I would say **screen campaigns** could go before the later robots arrive.
I would ask the owner for **written staffing plans**, not reassurance about my title.
think: I expect most **layout fees** and possibly my own wage to disappear.
I cannot fund a long search from **three weeks saved** and Eli’s uneven income.
do: Request **written bookings and staffing** now and list bus-reachable print shops.
Apply after most design work ends for a **posted paid print post**; keep offered agency hours.
Accept only **full-week wages and hours** covering rent and fares.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely wage loss with almost no buffer.
S2.quote: A master's degree cannot be cashed at the landlord's desk.
fieldNote: Her senior title offers **little protection** if the agency loses campaign fees.
She accepts a required **press-safety course** only for a posted paid role with shop-funded fees and paid training hours.

steps.text: Request written staffing plans and list print shops reachable by bus
Apply after most design work ends for posted paid print work; keep offered agency hours
Accept only written full-week wages and hours covering rent and bus fares
Take required press-safety course only for posted paid role with shop-funded fee and paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friends 2031 gives me time to learn what happens after a design file reaches the press. I would not tell them that five years makes the screen safe; robots reaching physical production around 2034 still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the agency may thin its design roster before full AGI arrives, and I need more than a new title on the same screen. The extra years let me test print work while my current wage still comes in, if someone will pay for that test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the local label printer for one paid observation shift and compare its actual rota with my rent and bus costs. If they offer it, I would learn safe finishing checks beside an operator; in the first year after 2031, if my design hours fall, I would apply for an advertised paid production opening only after seeing written weekly wages and hours that cover rent after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but less cornered than in 2028. A day beside the press would tell me whether the work is real or just a comforting word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would one shift make you qualified to run machinery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would start with checking labels and packing samples, not operating a press alone. A safe paid trial would tell me whether I want formal training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the printer offers an unpaid course instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my agency wage. I cannot use three weeks of savings to pay for several weeks without wages, even with five years to prepare.

say: I would say **five years** allows a real test of print production.
I would warn that **later robots** can also reach hands-on production.
think: I expect the **design roster** may thin before 2031.
I could test print work while wages arrive if a **paid shift** is offered.
do: Ask for one **paid observation shift** at the label printer and compare rota, rent and bus costs.
Learn **safe finishing checks** beside an operator only if that paid shift is offered.
Apply after 2031 design-hour cuts for an **advertised paid production role** with written after-travel rent-covering weekly terms.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but the longer warning leaves time for a paid test.
S3.quote: A day beside the press would tell me whether the work is real or just a comforting word.
fieldNote: A **paid observation**, not a training promise, tests whether the physical work suits her.
She does not claim a single shift qualifies her to **operate machinery**; rent and fare still set the wage gate.

steps.text: Ask label printer for paid observation shift; compare rota with rent and bus costs
Learn safe finishing checks beside operator only on offered paid shift
Keep agency wage instead of taking unpaid print course
Apply after 2031 cuts for advertised production with written after-travel rent-covering weekly terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the agency a decade is long enough to build a client list that does not vanish with one subscription. I would still talk about actual orders, not declare every future studio safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have paid down my rent arrears by then, or I might still be living one proof job at a time. I would rather own a small, dependable packaging relationship than chase a grand new design title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep my agency work and ask the owner whether I may take noncompeting local packaging jobs outside paid hours. If permitted, I would quote one bakery label only after getting the brief in writing and a deposit; I would put the paid profit into a rent reserve. In the first year after 2036, if agency work contracts, I would continue independent jobs only when signed orders cover the paper, travel and rent; I would not buy a press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about guessing ten years ahead, but glad there is time to build something slowly. One paid bakery label would mean more to me than ten imagined clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask the owner first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agency sometimes designs for food sellers, and I will not quietly take its customers. If the answer is no, I would keep the day job and build the cash buffer another way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a deposit protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paper samples and the bus fare to the bakery. Eli and I cannot afford to work for a warm thank-you while the rent date passes.

I would say a decade allows a **small client list** to grow slowly.
think: I want a **dependable packaging client**, not a grander screen title.
I may still have **rent pressure** despite a long warning.
do: Keep agency work and ask permission for **noncompeting packaging jobs** outside paid hours.
If permitted, quote one **bakery label** with written brief and deposit; save paid profit for rent.
After 2036 cuts, continue only **signed independent orders** covering paper, travel and rent; avoid buying a press.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about ten-year guesses but able to build slowly.
S4.quote: One paid bakery label would mean more to me than ten imagined clients.
fieldNote: Her side work is conditional on **agency permission** because food sellers overlap existing clients.

steps.text: Keep agency design work and seek permission for noncompeting packaging jobs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture. A written staffing date, a real paid print opening, and training hours that do not come out of my rent money would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays when a beautiful label is wrong. I am the person who stops a bad label before it reaches a shelf, but the agency pays me as if that were a small detail.

headlineQuote: I am the person who stops a bad label before it reaches a shelf, but the agency pays me as if that were a small detail.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old lead designer** with a master’s degree who checks food labels and clinic leaflets at a six-person agency.
Her **low pay** leaves three weeks saved, while her partner Eli’s café shifts vary.
She uses AI for **rough concepts** occasionally and judges new design systems by actual error checks.
Fast AGI threatens her **layout wage**; she considers paid print work and, with permission, a modest packaging client.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could erase most agency layout fees before she finds another rent-paying wage.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written staffing dates** and a real paid print opening.
Any required course needs **funded fees, paid hours** so rent money stays intact.
